group.passage:
In January 1692, mass hysteria broke out in Salem Village, Massachusetts. Two little girls, Elizabeth Parris, aged 9 and her cousin Abigail, aged 11, started having “fits.” They screamed, threw objects in uncontrollable rage, made strange noises and twisted themselves into strange positions. [[1]] The doctor concluded that they were bewitched, blaming their unexplainable behavior on the supernatural. When asked who had done this to them, Elizabeth and Abigail blamed three townswomen, including Tituba, a Native American slave who worked in their household. Tituba was known to have played fortune-telling games, which were forbidden by the Puritans. [[2]]
The three women were put in jail to await trial for practicing witchcraft. During the trial, Tituba confessed to having seen the devil, while Good and Osbourne claimed innocence. However, the court didn’t believe in their innocence, and all three women were hanged. [[3]] Many priests also encouraged their church followers to cast out the evil among them. Some accused individuals tried to save themselves from public humiliation by accusing their neighbors. Others who stood up for the defendants would likely be convicted of witchcraft themselves. Defendants were convicted with no evidence other than personal accusations. Spectral evidence — testimonies about dreams and visions — were allowed. [[4]] Women were not the only ones believed to be witches — men and children were accused too. By the end of the trials in 1693, 24 people had died, some in jail but most by hanging. The mass hysteria did not fade until the court declared the trials unlawful in 1703. However, it was not until more than 250 later that Massachusetts made a formal apology for the Salem Witch Trials.

options_bank.A: With the seed of paranoia planted, a stream of accusations followed for the next months.
options_bank.B: Concerned, Elizabeth’s father, Reverend Parris, brought in a doctor to examine the girls.
options_bank.C: Worse still, others were convicted simply because they failed the so-called “witch tests.”
options_bank.D: The other two accused women, Sarah Good and Sarah Osbourne, were not well liked by the community either.
